osces.title: Post-Extubation Respiratory Failure - Reintubation vs NIV Decision

scenario.clinicalVignette: Michael Chen, a 68-year-old man, was extubated 4 hours ago after 5 days of mechanical ventilation for community-acquired pneumonia. He is now developing respiratory distress with tachypnoea (RR 32/min), using accessory muscles, and oxygen saturations of 88% on 10L/min via Hudson mask. His wife is anxious, noting he looks worse than before intubation. ICU has one bed available.

tasks.description: Assess the patient's post-extubation respiratory failure
Interpret ABG and decide between NIV trial vs immediate reintubation
Communicate management plan to patient and family

physicalExamination.general: Alert but distressed, sitting upright, speaking in short phrases
physicalExamination.respiratory: Using accessory muscles, intercostal recession visible. Chest: bilateral coarse crackles in lower zones, reduced air entry right base. No wheeze.
physicalExamination.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, heart sounds dual with no murmurs, peripheral oedema absent
physicalExamination.neurological: GCS 15, no focal deficits, cough reflex intact but weak

investigations.result: pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L, BE +2, Lactate 2.8 mmol/L
Right lower lobe consolidation improving compared to 2 days ago, small right pleural effusion, no pneumothorax
WCC 12.8 x10⁹/L (neutrophils 10.2), Hb 108 g/L, Platelets 456 x10⁹/L
Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Cr 98 μmol/L, Urea 8.2 mmol/L, CRP 89 mg/L (down from 210)
245 pg/mL (mildly elevated)

immediate: Trial of NIV (BiPAP): IPAP 14 cmH2O, EPAP 6 cmH2O, FiO2 60%
Clear criteria for NIV failure: pH <7.25, inability to tolerate mask, deteriorating GCS
Prepare for reintubation if NIV fails within 1-2 hours
Nebulised salbutamol 5mg and ipratropium 500mcg
IV hydrocortisone 100mg stat
followUp: Speech pathology assessment for aspiration risk

expectedOutcomes.physiological: pH improvement >7.35, PaCO2 reduction <50 mmHg, PaO2 >70 mmHg on NIV within 2 hours
expectedOutcomes.clinical: Reduced work of breathing, RR <25/min, speaking in full sentences
expectedOutcomes.functional: Avoid reintubation in 60-70% of cases with early NIV

keyTeachingPoints: Post-extubation respiratory failure occurs in 10-20% of planned extubations
Early NIV can prevent reintubation in selected patients
Contraindications to NIV: facial trauma, vomiting, decreased GCS, haemodynamic instability
Close monitoring essential - delayed reintubation increases mortality
Consider causes: laryngeal oedema, diaphragm dysfunction, cardiac failure, aspiration
commonMistakes: Delaying NIV trial in appropriate candidates
Persisting with NIV when clear failure criteria met
Not preparing for urgent reintubation
Missing cardiac component of respiratory failure
Inadequate communication with family about treatment limitations

markingCriteria.criterion: Rapid systematic assessment of post-extubation failure
markingCriteria.details: Identifies respiratory acidosis, hypoxaemia, increased work of breathing
Recognises acute on chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoxaemia
BiPAP mode with appropriate IPAP/EPAP settings for CO2 clearance
pH threshold, GCS monitoring, tolerance assessment documented
ICU notification, equipment ready, team briefed
Bronchodilators, steroids, diuretics for fluid overload
1-hour ABG, continuous monitoring, clear escalation triggers
Explains situation, treatment options, potential outcomes clearly
Laryngeal oedema, aspiration, cardiac failure, diaphragm weakness
Clear plan, failure criteria, family discussion documented
Balances NIV trial with timely reintubation if needed

osces.title: Acute Chest Syndrome in Sickle Cell Disease - Exchange Transfusion

scenario.clinicalVignette: Fatima Okonkwo, a 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease (HbSS), presents with severe chest pain, fever, and increasing dyspnoea over 24 hours. She was admitted 2 days ago with vaso-occlusive crisis affecting her legs and back. Her regular haematologist is unavailable. SpO2 is 89% on 6L oxygen, and she appears very unwell.

patientInformation.name: Fatima Okonkwo
medicalHistory: Previous acute chest syndrome x3 (last episode 18 months ago)
Chronic pain syndrome - on regular oxycodone SR 20mg BD
Iron overload from transfusions - deferasirox 500mg daily
patientInformation.presentingComplaint: Severe pleuritic chest pain and worsening dyspnoea

tasks.description: Diagnose and assess severity of acute chest syndrome
Initiate immediate management including exchange transfusion decision
Coordinate with haematology and ICU for urgent exchange transfusion

physicalExamination.general: Distressed, using accessory muscles, unable to complete sentences
physicalExamination.respiratory: Decreased air entry right base and mid-zone, bronchial breathing right middle zone, dull percussion right base
physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, soft systolic flow murmur, no gallop, JVP not elevated
physicalExamination.abdomen: Soft, spleen palpable 2cm below costal margin (baseline), no hepatomegaly
physicalExamination.neurological: Alert but anxious, GCS 15, no focal neurological signs

investigations.result: New right middle and lower lobe consolidation, small right pleural effusion
pH 7.48, PaCO2 28 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L, SaO2 89%
Hb 68 g/L (baseline 75-80), WCC 24.6 x10⁹/L, Platelets 186 x10⁹/L, Reticulocytes 18%
Sickle cells ++, target cells +, Howell-Jolly bodies present
Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cr 142 μmol/L (baseline 90), Urea 11.2 mmol/L, Bilirubin 68 μmol/L (unconjugated), LDH 980 U/L
Blood group A positive, Antibody screen: Anti-C, Anti-E detected, 6 units matched blood available
Currently 78% (target <30% for acute chest syndrome)

immediate: High-flow nasal oxygen 60L/min, FiO2 60%
Urgent exchange transfusion - target HbS <30%, Hb 100-110 g/L
IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2g daily + azithromycin 500mg daily
Analgesia: morphine PCA with 1mg bolus, 5-minute lockout
IV fluids: careful hydration with normal saline 80mL/hour
Incentive spirometry every 2 hours while awake
followUp: Daily FBC, reticulocyte count, HbS percentage
Monitor for transfusion reactions given alloantibodies

expectedOutcomes.physiological: HbS <30% within 4-6 hours, improved oxygenation PaO2 >70 mmHg
expectedOutcomes.clinical: Resolution of chest pain, normalisation of respiratory rate <20/min
expectedOutcomes.functional: Prevention of multi-organ failure, avoiding mechanical ventilation

keyTeachingPoints: Acute chest syndrome is leading cause of death in sickle cell disease
Diagnostic criteria: new pulmonary infiltrate + fever/respiratory symptoms/chest pain
Exchange transfusion indicated for severe hypoxaemia (PaO2 <70 on air)
Target HbS <30% and Hb 100-110 g/L (avoid hyperviscosity)
Cover atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) with macrolide
Incentive spirometry reduces progression by preventing atelectasis
commonMistakes: Delayed recognition of acute chest syndrome
Simple transfusion instead of exchange (increases viscosity)
Over-hydration causing pulmonary oedema
Inadequate analgesia leading to splinting and atelectasis
Not covering atypical respiratory pathogens
Missing multi-organ involvement

markingCriteria.details: New infiltrate + respiratory symptoms in sickle cell patient
Severe hypoxaemia, multi-lobe involvement, haemodynamic compromise
CXR, ABG, FBC with reticulocytes, HbS%, cross-match
Incentive spirometry, VTE prophylaxis, careful fluid balance
Explains severity, treatment rationale to informed patient

osces.title: Eosinophilic Pneumonia - Steroid-Responsive Disease

scenario.clinicalVignette: Sarah Mitchell, a 42-year-old woman, presents with 3 weeks of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, night sweats, and 5kg weight loss. She started taking nitrofurantoin for a UTI 6 weeks ago. She has no history of asthma or allergies. CXR shows bilateral peripheral infiltrates. Her GP tried amoxicillin without improvement.

patientInformation.name: Sarah Mitchell
medicalHistory: Recurrent UTIs - 3 episodes in past year
patientInformation.presentingComplaint: Progressive breathlessness and dry cough for 3 weeks

tasks.description: Evaluate patient with suspected eosinophilic pneumonia
Initiate steroid therapy and monitoring plan

physicalExamination.general: Appears unwell, no acute distress, no rash or lymphadenopathy
physicalExamination.respiratory: Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles in upper and mid zones, no wheeze
physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physicalExamination.musculoskeletal: No joint swelling or muscle tenderness

investigations.result: Bilateral peripheral infiltrates, predominantly upper lobes, 'photographic negative' of pulmonary oedema pattern
WCC 16.4 x10⁹/L, Eosinophils 4.8 x10⁹/L (29%), Hb 118 g/L, Platelets 385 x10⁹/L
CRP 86 mg/L, ESR 62 mm/hr
Normal renal and liver function, Albumin 32 g/L
IgE 580 IU/mL (elevated), ANCA negative, Anti-nuclear antibody negative, Aspergillus-specific IgG negative
FEV1 2.1L (68% predicted), FVC 2.6L (71% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.81, DLCO 65% predicted
Bilateral ground-glass opacities with peripheral predominance, septal thickening, no bronchiectasis
BAL differential: Eosinophils 42%, Lymphocytes 18%, Neutrophils 8%, Macrophages 32%. No organisms seen.

immediate: Discontinue nitrofurantoin immediately
Commence prednisolone 50mg (0.75mg/kg) daily
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%
Monitor blood glucose given high-dose steroids
Baseline DEXA scan for bone density
followUp: Repeat CXR in 72 hours to assess response
FBC with eosinophil count weekly during steroid taper
Steroid taper: 40mg x 1 week, 30mg x 1 week, 20mg x 2 weeks, then reduce by 5mg weekly

expectedOutcomes.physiological: Rapid improvement in 48-72 hours, eosinophil count normalisation within 1 week
expectedOutcomes.clinical: Resolution of dyspnoea, improved exercise tolerance, weight gain
expectedOutcomes.functional: Return to work within 4-6 weeks, complete radiological resolution in 1-2 months

keyTeachingPoints: Eosinophilic pneumonia can be acute or chronic (CEP)
Drug-induced common: nitrofurantoin, NSAIDs, antibiotics, anticonvulsants
Peripheral blood eosinophilia not always present (BAL eosinophils >25% diagnostic)
Dramatic response to steroids within 48-72 hours is characteristic
Chronic form may relapse on steroid withdrawal - slow taper essential
Exclude parasitic infection and ABPA before steroids
commonMistakes: Treating as bacterial pneumonia without considering eosinophilic causes
Not checking medication history for causative drugs
Missing peripheral eosinophilia if only automated differential done
Tapering steroids too quickly leading to relapse
Not excluding other causes of pulmonary eosinophilia
Forgetting bone protection with prolonged steroids

markingCriteria.details: FBC with manual differential, CT chest, consideration of BAL
Stops nitrofurantoin, provides alternative for UTI prophylaxis
Gradual taper over 3-6 months to prevent relapse
Explains diagnosis, drug avoidance, steroid compliance

osces.title: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - BiPAP and Weight Loss

scenario.clinicalVignette: Robert Thompson, a 52-year-old truck driver, is brought to ED by his wife after she found him confused this morning. He has been increasingly sleepy over recent months, falling asleep at traffic lights. His BMI is 48 kg/m². He snores loudly and his wife reports breathing pauses at night. He has bilateral leg swelling and morning headaches.

patientInformation.name: Robert Thompson
medicalHistory: Never formally diagnosed with sleep apnoea
patientInformation.presentingComplaint: Morning confusion and excessive daytime sleepiness

tasks.description: Assess patient with suspected obesity hypoventilation syndrome
Interpret investigations and initiate BiPAP therapy
Develop comprehensive management plan including weight loss

physicalExamination.general: Obese, plethoric facies, drowsy but rousable, neck circumference 48cm
physicalExamination.respiratory: Reduced chest expansion, decreased air entry bibasally, no wheeze
physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Loud P2, RV heave at left sternal edge, bilateral pitting oedema to knees
physicalExamination.neurological: Drowsy, GCS 14 (E3, V5, M6), no focal deficits, asterixis present
physicalExamination.ENT: Crowded oropharynx (Mallampati class IV), large tongue, tonsillar hypertrophy

investigations.result: pH 7.32, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 34 mmol/L, BE +8
Hb 182 g/L (polycythaemia), Haematocrit 0.54, WCC 8.2 x10⁹/L, Platelets 234 x10⁹/L
Na 138 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, Cl 94 mmol/L, Urea 4.8 mmol/L, Cr 95 μmol/L
TSH 2.8 mIU/L, Free T4 14 pmol/L (normal)
Elevated hemidiaphragms, cardiomegaly, clear lung fields, no infiltrates
Right axis deviation, peaked P waves in II (P pulmonale), partial RBBB
Dilated right ventricle, RVSP 48 mmHg (pulmonary hypertension), normal LV function
FEV1 2.4L (68% predicted), FVC 2.9L (65% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.83

immediate: Commence BiPAP: IPAP 18 cmH2O, EPAP 8 cmH2O, backup rate 12
Target SpO2 88-92% (avoid over-oxygenation)
Admit to respiratory HDU for monitoring
Driving ban - notify transport authority
Urgent sleep study once stable
followUp: Sleep study with CO2 monitoring within 1 week
Respiratory clinic in 2 weeks with ABG on BiPAP
Dietitian referral for very low calorie diet program

expectedOutcomes.physiological: PaCO2 <50 mmHg within 3 months, improved daytime PaO2 >65 mmHg
expectedOutcomes.clinical: Resolution of morning headaches, improved alertness, reduced leg oedema
expectedOutcomes.functional: Potential return to driving after successful treatment (minimum 1 month)

keyTeachingPoints: OHS = obesity (BMI >30) + daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45) + no other cause
Distinguished from OSA by daytime hypercapnia (OSA has normal daytime PaCO2)
BiPAP preferred over CPAP due to chronic hypercapnia
Weight loss is crucial - 10% reduction significantly improves ventilation
Bariatric surgery most effective long-term treatment
Driving restrictions mandatory until treated - high accident risk
Avoid sedatives and excessive oxygen (can worsen hypercapnia)
commonMistakes: Using CPAP instead of BiPAP for hypercapnic respiratory failure
Over-oxygenating and suppressing respiratory drive
Not recognising cor pulmonale and right heart failure
Missing the diagnosis by not checking ABG in obese sleepy patients
Not addressing driving safety immediately
Focusing only on BiPAP without weight management plan

markingCriteria.details: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Correct mode choice (not CPAP), reasonable pressure settings
Sleep study, serial ABGs, BiPAP compliance
Weight loss importance, sleep hygiene, exercise
Clear plan, safety measures, follow-up arrangements

osces.title: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) - Young Woman with Recurrent Pneumothorax

scenario.clinicalVignette: Jessica Chen, a 34-year-old marketing manager, presents to ED with sudden right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. This is her third pneumothorax in 18 months. She has noticed increasing breathlessness on exertion over the past 2 years. She has never smoked. Her younger sister had a similar episode last year. She takes the oral contraceptive pill.

patientInformation.name: Jessica Chen
medicalHistory: Two previous right-sided pneumothoraces (18 and 10 months ago)
Sister age 29 - one pneumothorax, being investigated
patientInformation.presentingComplaint: Sudden right chest pain and breathlessness while exercising

tasks.description: Manage acute pneumothorax and investigate underlying cause
Develop long-term management plan including hormonal considerations

physicalExamination.general: Anxious, speaking in short sentences, no skin lesions or facial angiofibromas
physicalExamination.respiratory: Reduced chest expansion right side, hyperresonant percussion right chest, absent breath sounds right upper and mid zones
physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs
physicalExamination.abdomen: Soft, no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, no renal masses palpable

investigations.result: 30% right pneumothorax, hyperinflation, reticular pattern at bases bilaterally
Multiple thin-walled cysts throughout both lungs, predominantly 2-10mm diameter, no nodules, mild septal thickening
FEV1 2.1L (72% predicted), FVC 3.2L (88% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.66, RV 145% predicted
48% predicted (significantly reduced)
3,850 pg/mL (diagnostic threshold >800 pg/mL for LAM)
No angiomyolipomas, normal kidneys, normal pelvic organs
420 metres, desaturation to 86% on exertion
Normal level and phenotype
Estradiol 180 pmol/L, Progesterone 2.1 nmol/L (on OCP)

immediate: Intercostal catheter insertion - right 5th ICS mid-axillary line
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%
Analgesia - paracetamol 1g QID, oxycodone 5mg PRN
Chemical pleurodesis with talc after lung expansion
Cease oral contraceptive pill immediately

expectedOutcomes.physiological: Stabilisation of lung function decline with sirolimus (50% respond)
expectedOutcomes.clinical: Reduced pneumothorax recurrence with pleurodesis, improved exercise capacity
expectedOutcomes.functional: Maintain work capacity for several years, eventual transplant consideration

keyTeachingPoints: LAM affects women of childbearing age exclusively (oestrogen-dependent)
VEGF-D >800 pg/mL is diagnostic (avoids need for biopsy)
Sirolimus slows progression but doesn't cure - effect lost on cessation
Pregnancy accelerates disease - contraception crucial (progesterone-only)
Median transplant-free survival 15-20 years from symptom onset
Screen for tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) - 30% of TSC have LAM
Air travel increases pneumothorax risk - counsel appropriately
commonMistakes: Missing LAM diagnosis in young non-smoking women with pneumothorax
Continuing oestrogen-containing contraceptives
Not screening family members for LAM/TSC
Delaying pleurodesis after recurrent pneumothorax
Not starting sirolimus early in disease course
Missing early transplant referral opportunity
Inadequate counselling about pregnancy risks

markingCriteria.details: Recurrent pneumothorax in young woman prompts investigation
Cystic lung disease + elevated VEGF-D + clinical context
